Replacing Simulation with a Formula

Lesson 34 — Central Limit Theorem and t-statistics

Lt Col Cho

Four distributions we’ve seen

Distribution Values plotted Centered at Can we see it in practice?
Data distribution individual observations in one sample \bar{x} Yes
Sampling distribution a statistic (e.g., \bar{x}) from every possible sample of size n the parameter \mu No: requires many samples
Bootstrap distribution the statistic from resamples of the one sample the observed statistic Yes, by simulation
Null distribution the statistic from samples generated assuming H_0 the null value Yes, by simulation


  • The standard error (SE) of a statistic is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution.
  • The bootstrap approximates the spread and shape of the sampling distribution.
  • Can we estimate the sampling distribution without simulation?

Transition questions: what are the things you should know from a dead sleep (Empirical Rule, the four steps of a hypothesis test, and, after today, the CLT)? What happens to the spread of a statistic as n increases? How did we compute a p-value in a randomization test?

Draw the population circle with a sample coming out of it. The sampling distribution is the one we want and never observe. The bootstrap was our workaround: it is centered at our statistic, not the parameter, but its spread estimates the standard error. Most of the bootstrap and null distributions we simulated in Block 3 were symmetric and bell-shaped; that is not a coincidence. Answer to the closing question: yes, under conditions. The CLT gives the sampling distribution’s shape, center, and spread directly.

The Central Limit Theorem

If a sample consists of n independent observations from a population with mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma, and n is sufficiently large, then the sampling distribution of \bar{x} is approximately

\bar{x} \sim N\!\left(\text{mean} = \mu,\ \ \text{sd} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)

1. Shape

Approximately Normal. The approximation improves as n increases, whatever the shape of the population distribution.

2. Center

The population mean \mu.

3. Spread

Standard error \sigma / \sqrt{n}, which decreases as n increases.


  • The same result holds for a proportion \hat{p} (the mean of a variable coded 0 and 1) and for differences of two means or two proportions.
  • The CLT describes the distribution of sample means. The distribution of individual observations does not become Normal.

“Count to 3” when stating the CLT: shape, center, spread. Either the words or the symbols are acceptable on a GR. Ask: if n goes from 25 to 100, what happens to the standard error? It is cut in half, because the square root of n doubles. Show the Bunnies and Dragons video clip if you didn’t assign it.

The CLT for four statistics

  • Top: four populations. Bottom: the statistic from 10,000 random samples of each population. Blue curves: the Normal distribution the CLT gives (center = parameter, SD = SE).
\bar{x} \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \hat{p} \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2
Parameter 10 -2 0.30 0.15
Mean of the statistics 9.98 -1.99 0.300 0.150
SD of the statistics 1.57 1.44 0.046 0.079
SE from the CLT 1.58 1.44 0.046 0.078

Count to 3 with the picture, one column at a time. Shape: none of the four populations is Normal (right-skewed, uniform and bimodal, and two 0/1 variables), yet every bottom panel is approximately Normal. Center: the mean of the 10,000 statistics equals the parameter. Spread: the SD of the 10,000 statistics matches the SE formula (formulas on the standard-error slide). Ask: which population is farthest from Normal? The right-skewed one; its sample means still show slight right skew at n = 40. The online applet at onlinestatbook.com/stat_sim/sampling_dist lets cadets draw their own population shape.

Conditions for the CLT

  1. Independence. The observations are independent. A random sample or random assignment ensures this.
  2. Large enough sample. What counts as “large enough” depends on the statistic:
Statistic Large enough when…
Proportion \hat{p} at least 10 expected successes and 10 expected failures: np \geq 10 and n(1 - p) \geq 10
Mean \bar{x} small n: no clear outliers; large n: no particularly extreme outliers
guideline: slight skew is acceptable for n = 15, moderate skew for n = 30, strong skew for n = 60
Differences the condition holds in each group, and the groups are independent
  • n \geq 30 is a guideline, not a guarantee: for a population with extreme outliers, the sampling distribution of \bar{x} can remain skewed at n = 100 or larger.

A small sample from an approximately Normal population is fine; a sample of 30 from a population with extreme outliers may not be. For proportions, use the null value p0 in the success-failure check for a test, and p-hat for a confidence interval. Independence is about how the data were collected; no sample size fixes dependent data.

The spread: standard error

  • The standard error (SE) of a statistic is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution: the “spread” in the CLT.
  • The CLT gives each SE in terms of population values, which are unknown, so we substitute sample values:
Statistic SE from the CLT Estimated SE
\bar{x} \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\hat{p} \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}} \sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}
\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}} \sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}}
\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \sqrt{\dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}} \sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}
  • Proportion: the SE depends only on p. Under H_0: p = p_0 the SE is known: \sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}.
  • Mean: the SE depends on \sigma, which H_0: \mu = \mu_0 does not specify. The SE must be estimated with s.

You do not need to memorize these formulas; identify which one applies and use it. For differences the variances add, because both statistics vary from sample to sample. The last two bullets set up the next two slides: a known SE leads to Z, an estimated SE leads to T. For two proportions, H0: p1 = p2 doesn’t give the common value, so the test estimates it with the pooled proportion (the overall proportion of successes).

From the CLT to Z and T

  • The CLT gives the null distribution of \hat{p}. How do we measure how far the observed \hat{p} is from p_0?
  • Example: H_0: p = 0.50, n = 100, observed \hat{p} = 0.58. SE under H_0: \sqrt{0.50 \cdot 0.50 / 100} = 0.05.
  • Subtracting a constant shifts the axis, and dividing by a constant rescales it. The shape and the shaded area, P(\hat{p} \geq 0.58) = 0.055, are the same in all three panels.
  • After step 3, every test uses one reference distribution, N(0, 1), and the value is the number of SEs between the statistic and the null value.
  • Step 3 requires the SE. For \hat{p}, H_0 specifies p_0, so the SE is known: this gives Z. For \bar{x}, the SE is \sigma/\sqrt{n} and \sigma is unknown; replacing \sigma with s gives T.

Open with the randomization-test callback: we used to locate the observed statistic in a simulated null distribution. Now the CLT hands us that distribution as a Normal curve. Walk the three panels left to right: same curve, same shaded area, only the numbers on the axis change. Ask: in panel 3, what does 1.6 mean? (p-hat is 1.6 standard errors above the null value.) Connect to the Block 1 Z score, (x - mu)/sigma: same operation applied to a statistic, with the SE in place of the SD. Why bother: one table/one R function (pnorm) for every problem instead of a new Normal curve for every p0 and n. The last bullet previews the next two slides.

Standardizing with a known SE: Z

Z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}} \qquad\qquad Z \sim N(0, 1) \ \text{ approximately, if } H_0 \text{ is true}

  • \hat{p}: the sample proportion. p_0: the value of p stated in H_0 (the null value). n: the sample size.
  • Z is the number of standard errors \hat{p} lies above (positive) or below (negative) p_0: the Block 1 Z score, with the SE in place of the SD. Under H_0 the SE is known, and by the CLT Z follows the standard Normal distribution. In R: pnorm(z) is the area to the left of z.
\hat{p} Z
Name test statistic standardized statistic
Center under H_0 p_0 0

Open with: in a randomization test, how did we decide whether the observed statistic was far from the null value? Before, we located it in a simulated null distribution. Now the CLT says the null distribution of p-hat is approximately Normal, centered at p0, with spread equal to the SE, so subtracting p0 and dividing by the SE puts every problem on the same N(0, 1) scale. Ask: how unusual is a statistic 2 SEs from the null value? 3 SEs? (Beyond 3: about 0.3% of the time, in either direction.) The shaded bands are the Empirical Rule. Mnemonic: pnorm and “probability” both start with “puh.” The same construction gives Z for two proportions (next slides show it in a table).

Standardizing with an estimated SE: T

T = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} \qquad\qquad T \sim t_{n-1} \ \text{ approximately, if } H_0 \text{ is true}

  • \bar{x}: the sample mean. \mu_0: the value of \mu stated in H_0 (the null value). s: the sample SD. n: the sample size.
  • s varies from sample to sample, so T varies more than Z. The t-distribution has heavier tails to account for that additional variability. One parameter: degrees of freedom, df = n - 1 for one mean (t_{n-1} denotes t with df = n - 1). As df increases, t approaches the standard Normal. In R: pt(t, df).
Z T
SE uses a known value (\sigma or p_0) the sample SD s
Used for proportions means (and regression slopes, Lesson 35)

Numbers to quote: the probability of falling more than 3 units from 0 is 0.0027 for the Normal and 0.0955 for t with df = 2. For df of about 30 or more, t and Normal are nearly indistinguishable. Precise point if asked: replacing sigma with s does not change the distribution of x-bar; it changes the distribution of the standardized statistic T. History: William Sealy Gosset developed the t-distribution for quality control at the Guinness brewery and published under the name “Student.”

Hypothesis tests with a mathematical model

  • The four steps are unchanged. Step 3 uses the Normal or t curve instead of a simulated null distribution, and the p-value is the area under the curve at least as extreme as Z or T.
H_0 Standardized statistic Distribution under H_0
\mu = \mu_0 T = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} t, df = n - 1
p = p_0 Z = \dfrac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}} standard Normal
\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 T = \dfrac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - 0}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2}} t, df = \min(n_1, n_2) - 1
p_1 - p_2 = 0 Z = \dfrac{(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) - 0}{\sqrt{\hat{p}_{pool}(1-\hat{p}_{pool})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}} standard Normal
  • Every row has the same form: (statistic − null value) / SE. The SE uses the null value wherever H_0 specifies one.

You do not memorize this table. The pooled proportion is the overall proportion of successes in both groups combined; it estimates the common p that H0 assumes. min(n1, n2) - 1 is a conservative stand-in for the degrees of freedom that software computes. Two-sided p-value: double the one-tail area.

One-mean t-test: gnome sleep

  • Claim: gnomes sleep 145 minutes per night on average. A random sample of n = 64 USAFA gnomes has \bar{x} = 135 and s = 16 minutes. Do USAFA gnomes sleep less on average?
Step
0 \alpha = 0.05
1 H_0: \mu = 145 vs. H_A: \mu < 145
2 Test statistic: \bar{x} = 135
3 Conditions: random sample (independence); n = 64, no extreme outliers
SE = \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \dfrac{16}{\sqrt{64}} = 2
T = \dfrac{135 - 145}{2} = -5, with df = n - 1 = 63
p-value = pt(-5, df = 63) = 2.4 \times 10^{-6}
  • What does T = -5 mean? What would we have done with simulation?

T = -5: the sample mean is 5 standard errors below the null value 145. Empirical Rule: about 0.15% of a Normal distribution lies more than 3 SEs below the mean, so the p-value is below 0.0015 even without software. With simulation we would have generated sample means assuming mu = 145 and counted the proportion at or below 135. pt() gives the left-tail area, which matches H_A: mu < 145.

Gnome sleep: the p-value as an area

Step 4: p-value < 0.001 < \alpha = 0.05. Reject H_0: the data provide statistically discernible evidence that USAFA gnomes sleep less than 145 minutes per night on average.

The shaded area is the p-value; it is too small to see. The top axis is the standardized scale, the bottom axis the original scale; they describe the same curve. The curve plays the role the simulated null distribution played in Block 3: instead of counting simulated means at or below 135, we compute the area under the curve.

One-proportion Z-test: marijuana legalization

  • A General Social Survey random sample of 1,563 US adults: 60% said marijuana should be legal. Is the population proportion greater than 0.50?
Step
0–1 \alpha = 0.05; H_0: p = 0.50 vs. H_A: p > 0.50
2 Test statistic: \hat{p} = 0.60
3 Conditions: random sample; np_0 = n(1 - p_0) = 781.5 \geq 10
SE = \sqrt{\dfrac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.5(0.5)}{1563}} = 0.01265 (uses p_0: the test assumes H_0)
Z = \dfrac{0.60 - 0.50}{0.01265} = 7.91; p-value = pnorm(7.91, lower.tail = FALSE) < 0.001
4 Reject H_0: statistically discernible evidence that more than half of US adults think marijuana should be legal

Ask: is 60% a statistic or a parameter? A statistic: it was computed from the 1,563 respondents. Z = 7.91: the sample proportion is about 8 standard errors above 0.50, far beyond anything the Empirical Rule calls plausible. This is a Z-test, not a t-test: under H0 the standard error is computed from p0, so no standard deviation has to be estimated.

When the Normal model does not fit

  • A medical consultant: 3 of 62 clients had complications (\hat{p} = 0.048). Is the complication rate below the typical p_0 = 0.10?
Simulated null distribution Normal model
p-value 0.123 0.088
  • Check the success-failure condition. Why do the two p-values differ?

np0 = 62(0.10) = 6.2, fewer than 10 expected successes, so the condition fails. The simulated null distribution (grey bars, 10,000 simulated samples) is right-skewed and takes only a few distinct values; the Normal curve (blue) does not match it, and its p-value is about 30% smaller than the simulation’s. In IMS’s other example (the opportunity cost study) the conditions hold and the two methods give p-values of 0.0052 and 0.006. The method is only as good as its conditions.

Confidence intervals with a mathematical model

\text{point estimate} \pm \underbrace{(\text{critical value}) \times SE}_{\text{margin of error}} \qquad \bar{x} \pm t^\star_{n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \qquad \hat{p} \pm z^\star\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}

  • The critical value is the number of SEs that captures the middle X% of the Normal (z^\star) or t (t^\star) distribution. Use t^\star for means and z^\star for proportions.
  • An interval has no null value, so a proportion’s SE uses \hat{p}.
Confidence level z^\star (Normal) t^\star, df = 30
90% 1.645 1.697
95% 1.960 2.042
99% 2.576 2.750 
qnorm(0.975)          # cutoff with 97.5% of the Normal curve below it
qt(0.975, df = 30)    # the same cutoff for t with 30 df

Empirical Rule version: a 95% interval is about the estimate plus or minus 2 SE. Mnemonic: qnorm and “cutoff” both start with a “kuh” sound. Ask: why is t-star larger than z-star at every level? Heavier tails: you have to go farther out to capture the middle 95%. For 95%, use 0.975: 2.5% in each tail.

Confidence intervals: gnome sleep

Gnomes: \bar{x} = 135 and s = 16 in both samples.

  • How do the intervals change with the confidence level? With the sample size? Is 145 plausible?

The 95% interval is wider than the 68% interval: more confidence requires a wider interval. The n = 16 intervals are twice as wide as the n = 64 intervals (SE 4 vs. 2), and slightly more because t-star with 15 df is larger. 145 is outside every interval, consistent with rejecting H0. Interpretation: we are 95% confident that the mean sleep of USAFA gnomes is between 131 and 139 minutes per night (n = 64). The 95% describes the method: about 95% of intervals constructed this way capture mu.

Confidence interval: marijuana legalization

  • Marijuana survey: \hat{p} = 0.60, n = 1,563.

0.60 \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.60(0.40)}{1563}} = 0.60 \pm 1.96(0.0124) = (0.576,\ 0.624)

  • The interval uses \hat{p} in the standard error. The test used p_0, because the test assumes H_0; an interval has no null value.
  • A headline states: “Majority of US adults think marijuana should be legalized.” Does the interval support the headline?
  • How would the interval change for a 99% confidence level? For a sample of 6,000 adults?

Interpretation: we are 95% confident that the proportion of all US adults who think marijuana should be legal is between 0.576 and 0.624. Every value in the interval is above 0.50, so the headline is supported. 99%: wider (z-star 2.576 instead of 1.96). Larger sample: narrower, because n is in the denominator of the SE.

Simulation or mathematical model?

Step Simulation-based Mathematical model-based
0–1. \alpha, hypotheses same same
2. Observed statistic same same, plus its standardized value (Z or T)
3. Null distribution simulate assuming H_0 Normal or t curve from the CLT
3. p-value proportion of simulated statistics at least as extreme area under the curve beyond Z or T
4. Conclusion same same
Confidence interval middle X% of the bootstrap distribution estimate \pm critical value \times SE
  • Mathematical models: no simulation and closed-form formulas, but only valid when the conditions hold, and available only for certain statistics (means, proportions, their differences, and regression coefficients).
  • Simulation: works for other statistics (medians, standard deviations), but still requires independent observations and a representative sample.
  • Neither method corrects biased sampling, confounding, or dependent observations.

The logic of inference is unchanged; only Step 3 and the way the CI is built change. Bootstrapping does not fix a small sample: with very few observations the bootstrap distribution is also a poor approximation.

Practice: fuel efficiency

City fuel efficiency (mpg) for random samples of 2021 cars:

Transmission Mean SD n
Manual 22.7 4.58 25
Automatic 17.4 3.44 25

Do the data provide statistically discernible evidence of a difference in mean city mileage? Use \alpha = 0.05.

  1. State H_0 and H_A.
  2. Check the conditions.
  3. Compute the test statistic, the standard error, and T. What degrees of freedom do you use?
  4. Find the p-value with R and state a conclusion in context.

Answers: (1) H0: mu_manual - mu_auto = 0; HA: mu_manual - mu_auto is not 0. (2) Independent random samples; 25 per group, and the textbook’s box plots show roughly symmetric data with no extreme outliers. (3) Difference 22.7 - 17.4 = 5.3 mpg; SE = sqrt(4.58^2/25 + 3.44^2/25) = 1.146; T = 4.63; df = min(25, 25) - 1 = 24. (4) p-value = 2 * pt(-4.63, df = 24) = 0.0001. Reject H0: statistically discernible evidence that mean city mileage differs between manual and automatic transmissions.

Practice: working backwards

  1. A 90% t-interval for a population mean, based on a random sample of 25 observations, is (65, 77). Find the sample mean, the margin of error, and the sample standard deviation.

  2. H_0: \mu = 60 vs. H_A: \mu \neq 60, with s = 8 and n = 20. For what sample mean(s) would the p-value equal 0.05?

  3. Complete the sentence: as the sample size increases, the standard error ______ and the sampling distribution becomes ______.

  1. x-bar = 71 (the midpoint); MOE = 6 (half the width); t-star = qt(0.95, 24) = 1.711; 6 = 1.711 * s / 5, so s = 17.5. (2) Two-sided p-value 0.05 means |T| = qt(0.975, 19) = 2.093, so x-bar = 60 plus or minus 2.093 * 8 / sqrt(20) = 56.26 or 63.74 (both). (3) decreases; narrower (and closer to Normal).
